Open Start and type your company name and your own limits in the yellow cells: the repair allowance, the days a repair should take, the approval limit and the warning days for policies, tax bills and warranties.

Record every repair on Work orders with the property, the kind, the priority, the vendor and the cost. Days to fix, the days a job has waited and a speed check fill in, and open jobs past your limit turn red.

List every big item on Capex plan (capex means big repairs and replacements) with its planned year, life and cost. The shortfall and the monthly saving needed fill in, and Reserve deposits keeps the money you set aside.
Use Repair or replace for items that keep failing and Repair costs by kind to see where the money goes. Tenant-caused repairs keeps the cost, the deposit and what you recovered.

Keep every policy on Insurance policies with the premium, the deductible (the part of a claim you pay yourself) and the renewal date, and every claim on Insurance claims. Policies renewing soon turn amber.
Enter each property tax bill with its due date. Open bills show the days left and late payments are counted. Check your own local rules for due dates and appeals.
Track Warranties, Safety checks, Recurring service, Property inspections and the Emergency log so no date is missed. Check your own local rules for the safety checks you must do.
Rate your Vendors out of 5 and read their jobs and spend. Properties shows the repair cost against the allowance, the capex shortfall, the premium and the last inspection score for each property.
Use the 14 calculators: repair or replace, capex reserve, reserve funding, cost per unit, budget by age, quotes, emergency bill, insurance, tax appeal, life left, damage and a grid.
Read the Maintenance and Capex Dashboard and Charts every week: open work orders, repair cost, capex shortfall, renewals, tax bills and overdue safety checks.
Figures about tax, insurance and repairs are not legal or tax advice: check your own local rules and check with your own adviser before you act on them.

Properties: value, loan, equity and cash flow
The 16 properties with price and value; rent roll (the list of units, tenants and rents), cash flow of the last 12 months, loan balance, equity and LTV (loan divided by value) fill in.
Underwriting: what each property was expected to earn
One row for each held property with the rent, the vacancy and the yearly costs used at purchase; NOI, cash flow, cap rate, cash-on-cash and DSCR expected fill in.
Property months: rent, costs and loan payments by month
One row for each property and month with the rent collected, each cost and the loan payments; operating costs, NOI (rent collected minus operating costs, before loan payments) and cash flow fill in.
Rent payments: what each unit owed and paid
One row for each unit and month with the rent due and the amount paid; the amount still owed and a payment check fill in.
Expenses: every cost line of every property
One row for each cost with the property, the category and the amount; the same category cost of the last 12 months fills in so a bill can be judged against the year.
Loan payments: payment, interest and balance each month
One row for each loan payment with the interest and the principal; the share that is interest and whether the loan only pays interest fill in.
Loans: payment, balance and balloon date
One row for each loan; the payment, the balance today, the yearly loan payments, LTV, the days to a balloon (a loan whose remaining balance is due on one date) and the DSCR of the property fill in.
Valuations: what each property was worth and when
One row for each opinion of value with the source; the gain against the purchase price fills in.
Rent units: the units behind the rent
One row for each rental unit with the tenant and the rent; the market rent and the gap to it fill in from Rent against market.
Budget by property: yearly budget and actual by category
One row for each property and cost category with the yearly budget and the actual cost; the variance, the share over budget and a budget check fill in.
Cash invested: the cash you put into each property
One row for each held property with the down payment, the closing costs and the rehab paid in cash; total cash in, the cash flow of a year and the payback years fill in.
Property results: the last 12 months against the targets
One row for each held property; the last 12 months fill in from Property months: NOI, cap rate, cash-on-cash, DSCR, return on equity, rank and the keep, fix or sell signal.
Expense ratios: each cost as a share of rent
One row for each property type and cost category with the share of rent in the last 12 months and your benchmark; the gap and a check fill in.
Benchmarks: the targets you judge each property by
The eight shares you use as targets for cap rate, return, costs and vacancy; change them to your own.
Rent against market: what each unit could rent for
One row for each unit with the market rent you found; the rent charged, the gap, the gap a year and a market check fill in. Units below market by more than your limit turn amber.
Action list: what to do about each finding
One row for each finding with the action, the owner and the due date; open or closed, the days left and an overdue check fill in. Only open items can be overdue.
Performance reviews: a rating for each property each quarter
One row for each review with a rating from 1 to 5 and a note; a strong, fair or weak check fills in.
Rate and value changes: what each change did
One row for each change in a loan rate or in a value; the yearly cash flow effect of a rate change and a cost check fill in.

Actual against underwriting: rent, costs and cash flow
Type what you expected when you bought and what happened over the year; see the variance of rent, costs and cash flow, and whether rent or costs caused the gap.
Expense ratio check: a cost against rent and your benchmark
Type one cost of a year, the rent of a year and your benchmark share; see the share of rent, the gap and the saving that reaches the benchmark.
Operating expense reduction: the effect on NOI and value
Type the cost of one category, the saving you expect, the NOI and the cap rate; see the yearly effect on NOI and the value it adds (a saving is worth the saving divided by the cap rate).

Vacancy effect on NOI and cash flow
Type the rent when full, the vacancy now and a new vacancy, the costs and the loan payments; see how NOI, cash flow and DSCR change.
Keep, fix or sell signal for one property
Type the cash-on-cash return, the equity, the repairs needed and the cap rate; see whether to keep it, fix it first or review it for a sale. Check with your own adviser before you sell.

Return on equity: the return on what is left in the property
Type the equity, the cash flow of a year and the value gain; see the return on the equity (cash flow plus value gain, divided by the equity) against the return on the cash you first put in.
Type the costs, the loan payments, the units and the vacancy; see the rent for each unit a month that covers everything and your margin over it.

Debt service coverage with a rate rise
Type the NOI, the loan, the rate now, a higher rate and the years left; see the payment after the rise and the coverage (DSCR: NOI divided by loan payments) against your minimum.
Loan payments after the rise a year
NOI needed for the minimum DSCR
Portfolio ranking score for one property
Type the cash-on-cash return, the DSCR, the return on equity and the cash flow margin; see a score of 100 (35 for return, 25 for DSCR, 20 for equity return and 20 for margin) to rank your properties.
What-if grid: rent against cost ratio for cash flow
Type the rent roll of a year, the cost ratio, the loan payments and the value; each row of the grid shows the cash flow when the rent or the cost ratio changes.
